title: Ben Pollack as drummer; Glenn Miller on Johnny Dodds
summary: Freeman calls Pollack one of the first to understand jazz; Miller, who knew no early jazz, took offense at praise of Johnny Dodds in front of Goodman.

story.theme_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the leader and his bands
story.community_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the perfectionist bandleader

blocks.x: Well, I will tell you what, I think we ought to go back a second there, because actually from a jazz point of view, you pardon me, we take all the misery out of that word. It's got to be used, you got to express yourself for what you mean.
So, forgive. So, from a jazz point of view, Ben Pollack is a lot more interesting to me. than Tommy Dorsey.
Oh, Ben Pollack was a marvelous drummer, and he was one of the first people to understand jazz and he was one of the first men to hear King Oliver and Baby Dodds.

I remember one night he was telling -- just happened to mentioned to Glenn Miller that he thought Johnny Dodds was a great clarinet player and Glenn Miller was insulted. He said, 'How dare you say that in the presence of Benny Goodman.' They had a big argument and I wanted to break in, but I was new in the band, so I didn't.
And Glenn Miller just stood there -- he was a Denver guy, he didn't know anything about the early jazz.
He thought that Benny Goodman was the first jazz clarinet player that ever lived. True enough, Benny Goodman was a great artist, we all know that.
That is needless to say, but God, there were guys that played clarinet before Goodman that really --
Well, I am surprised Benny didn't speak up because he knew about Jimmy Dodds -- Johnny Dodds, and Jimmy Noone -- the same thing.
